newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan offers investors its stake in tobacco firm.
newsitem.headline: Jordan offers investors its stake in tobacco firm.

text.p: Jordan's state investment arm said on Saturday it was seeking bids from investors to buy a 13.3 percent shareholding in Jordan Tobacco and Cigarettes Company.

Jordan Investment Corporation (JIC) said it was auctioning its 40,000 shares in the company which manufactures brand name cigarettes under license with offers accepted for purchase of at least 10,000 shares, an official said.
JIC sold at the end of last year its remaining 32.7 percent share in Jordan Hotels and Tourism Company to a group of local investors in a deal estimated at around 12.5 million dinars ($17.6 million).
An original 62.3 percent of JIC's holding in the hotel firm, which owns Jordan's Intercontinental Hotel, was sold in 1995 to the tourism holding group Zara Investments.
JIC owns parts of around 70 public shareholding companies with an estimated market value of around 500 million dinars ($706 million).
Investors say concrete steps to move ahead in selloffs of JIC's holdings in profitable majority state owned concerns, are essential to show seriousness in privatisation plans.
They say success of the country's IMF directed expanded reforms depends on an accelerated sell-off programme.
JIC has so far only sold some shares in the Philadelphia Hotel while it failed in selling a sizeable holding in Arab International Hotel which owns the Marriott Hotel.
But despite pledges to the IMF, Jordan has not embarked on a systematic plan of selloffs of profitable state concerns or large stakes in firms listed in the stock market.
Its vanguard move so far has been its decision to sell a 26 percent stake in its profitable state telecomms body to a strategic foreign investor by year end.
Financial analysts say what could attract foreign interest is offering JIC's sizeable stakes in Jordan's potash and phosphate industry, which however it is reluctant to consider at this stage.

JIC said that it will re-tender soon to foreign investors an offer to lease Maeen hot spring resort while it has put off a decision to sell a 20 percent stake in Jordan Cement Factories until the government takes steps to deregulate cement prices.
Investors criticise a piecemeal privatisation approach and say even the so far limited selloffs should be through the stock market rather than by private auctions.
